title: Writing Core Tests
hints: A unit test extends TYPO3\TestingFramework\Core\Unit\UnitTestCase, a functional test TYPO3\TestingFramework\Core\Functional\FunctionalTestCase. Both are final and mark cases with the #[Test] attribute rather than a test method-name prefix.

A functional test declares its environment through properties: protected array $coreExtensionsToLoad, $testExtensionsToLoad and $configurationToUseInTestInstance. Load only what the test needs — every extension costs setup time per test class.

A functional test starts on an empty database: the first test of a class installs the schema and no rows, every test after it is preceded by a truncation of all tables, and the framework imports nothing of its own — so the only records a test run sees are the ones it primed. A record nobody imported is absent rather than stale: setUpBackendUser(1) fails with "does not exist in the database" until a be_users fixture is imported. Two things change that — protected bool $initializeDatabase = false skips creation and truncation entirely, and withDatabaseSnapshot() carries rows the first test of a class created past the truncation for the rest of it.

State is set up and asserted with CSV fixtures, not hand-written inserts: $this->importCSVDataSet(__DIR__ . '/Fixtures/pages.csv') in setUp(), $this->assertCSVDataSet(__DIR__ . '/Fixtures/Expected.csv') for the result. The files live in a Fixtures/ directory next to the test class. This is the expected form for persistence behaviour.
Take services from the container with $this->get(SomeService::class) rather than constructing them, so the test exercises the real wiring.

hints.text: Tests mirror the class path: typo3/sysext/<ext>/Classes/Foo/Bar.php is tested by typo3/sysext/<ext>/Tests/{Unit,Functional}/Foo/BarTest.php.

hints: The name says what holds and the comment says which case is exercised: typeSpecificTitleOverridesCtrlTitle, and a docblock naming the path the case takes and why that path matters. Neither carries the issue number — no test method in the core's system extensions is named after one, and the number is already in the commit's Resolves: trailer and in the changelog file name. "Regression test for #N" dates the test to the fix it came out of and says nothing a reader needs years later, which is when a test is read.
Run the single test file or method while iterating; a full functional run costs minutes per round. typo3_test_run_guide has the targeted invocation.

hints.text: A change that alters rendered output — a URI, a tag, an attribute other tests assert verbatim — is asserted far outside the class's own test, and one search finds those expectations if it is aimed correctly. Search the whole typo3/sysext/*/Tests/ tree rather than *Test.php: roughly half the files holding such an expectation are fixtures the test loads instead of asserting inline — Fixtures/*.php returning a heredoc, .csv, .xml, .typoscript, .html, and a quoted-printable .message. And search for the stable text around the value rather than the value itself, because the value is escaped in a PCRE ('\.jpg', '\?\d+'), split across a sprintf() format ('@^

hints: Output the pipeline determines whole is asserted whole, with assertSame against the full serialized string: an escape, an attribute order or a namespace that moves is then a failure, and a containsString check passes all three. That is what a sanitiser is worth testing for, and the core's own SvgSanitizer suite asserts with contains, so the shape is not read off the neighbours. Where the string carries a value the change does not decide, the assertion is on the part that is — icon markup embeds the published asset path, and the publisher names that directory by a package hash, so pinning it whole fails on the next unrelated republish.

Write the narrowest test that exercises the change, and let what the change touches decide the kind: isolated logic is a unit test, while service wiring, persistence, TCA, DataHandler, routing and anything reading configuration only behave like themselves in a functional test. A unit test of those asserts the mock.

A backend route in a test is TYPO3\CMS\Backend\Routing\Route, which takes a path and options; the core class of the same name takes defaults before its options. Built from the wrong one, getOption() answers null with no error and the test passes without reaching what it is named after.

hints.text: A functional test that loads EXT:core/Tests/Functional/Fixtures/Frontend/JsonRenderer.typoscript can observe nothing the PageRenderer assembles. That file is the shared base the SiteHandling and DataScenarios tests build their site on, with a fixture of their own layered over it, and it sets config.disableAllHeaderCode = 1 — so RequestHandler::generatePageContent() returns the body before the renderer is populated. No assertion in such a test can fail on a meta tag, a stylesheet, a script or the page title, whatever the change did to them, and a test about any of those needs a TypoScript fixture that does not include that base. frontend-render-pipeline-state is where that phase sits.

title: Setting a Test Suite Up in an Extension
appliesTo: the functional suite will not start
This version of PHPUnit requires PHP
site set in a functional test
assert the rendered output of a content element
hints: Two questions live here: a declared suite that will not start, which is the credentials, the account and the interpreter; and a harness that does not exist yet, which starts at the copied configuration files.

A functional run needs database credentials in the environment: typo3DatabaseDriver, typo3DatabaseHost, typo3DatabaseName, typo3DatabaseUsername, typo3DatabasePassword. Without them it stops with "Database credentials for tests are neither set through environment variables, and can not be found in an existing LocalConfiguration file", which does not name the variables it is missing.

Every test class gets a database of its own — the configured name plus a hash of the class — so that account has to be allowed to create databases. Under DDEV that means root rather than the user the site itself runs as.

PHPUnit checks the interpreter itself, before the autoloader and so before composer/platform_check.php: it stops with "This version of PHPUnit requires PHP" and the version it wants. Composer resolved that PHPUnit against the PHP that ran composer, so an install run on the host can pick one the container cannot start.

Two things send the run to the host instead. .ddev/config.yaml is tracked, so from a git worktree ddev exec and ddev describe both stop with "a project (web container) in running state already exists", and the container has the original checkout mounted rather than the worktree. The other is that interpreter. Either one is run against the database DDEV publishes: ddev describe -j carries raw.dbinfo.published_port, assigned at start unless host_db_port pins it, and Testbase reads typo3DatabasePort beside the credentials above.

Nothing drops one after the run ends. The only drop is at the start of that class's first test — Testbase::setUpTestDatabase() drops the name where it exists, then creates it again — and tearDown() removes a site configuration directory and one cache file and nothing else. No tearDownAfterClass() is declared anywhere, so a finished suite leaves one database per test class that ran, beside a typo3temp/var/tests/functional-<7 hex> instance directory each, and each of them is reclaimed only when that same class runs again. The hash is substr(sha1(<test class>), 0, 7) rather than a per-run value, so the set is bounded by the test classes instead of growing with every run, and no leftover is ever read again: dropping all of them costs the next run nothing.

A functional test runs with the working directory at that instance directory: Testbase::setUpInstanceCoreLinks() calls chdir($instancePath) on the first test of each test case class, and nothing changes it back. Environment::getPublicPath() resolves to the same path, so a test never sees the project root a CLI call starts in. A test about relative path resolution has to move the working directory itself and restore it in a finally block, or it passes with the defect it is meant to prove.

That _ft<7 hex> suffix is the whole of what tells a leftover from the live database, and it exists only under a server driver. The connection is repointed to <typo3DatabaseName>_ft<7 hex> before the instance boots, so nothing a functional test writes reaches the configured database — a row that changed there was changed outside the test run. Two cases carry no such name at all: protected bool $initializeDatabase = false on the class creates no database, and under pdo_sqlite the per-class database is the file typo3temp/var/tests/functional-sqlite-dbs/test_<7 hex>.sqlite with an .empty.sqlite beside it, where deleting that directory is the cleanup.

hints.text: A site the fixture names its sets in renders in a functional test as if it named none: `setUpFrontendRootPage()` writes a sys_template row with clear = 3, `SysTemplateTreeBuilder` adds the site's own include ahead of every row, and `IncludeTreeAstBuilderVisitor` resets the whole AST for the first row carrying that flag — so the sets are included and then discarded. The frontend then answers "Content Element with uid <n> and type <ctype> has no rendering definition!", which reads as a site set that was never resolved. Import the element's own TypoScript file into the fixture setup.typoscript instead, together with the helper it copies from, and the constants those files read stay unresolved without stopping the assertion.

hints: The conventions of a core test hold here — UnitTestCase, FunctionalTestCase, final classes, #[Test], CSV fixtures, $this->get() for services — but the harness they run in does not exist yet and is the whole first day.

typo3/testing-framework ships UnitTests.xml and FunctionalTests.xml under Resources/Core/Build/, and the files say in their own header that extensions should copy them rather than reference them: their testsuite directory points into the core mono repository. Copy those two to Build/ in the extension, point each testsuite at Tests/Unit/ and Tests/Functional/, and run them as vendor/bin/phpunit -c Build/UnitTests.xml. There is no runTests.sh outside the core.

The two bootstraps beside them are the exception: they hold nothing an extension configures — a Testbase, ORIGINAL_ROOT and two directories created below typo3temp/var/ — so copying them buys a file nobody updates. Point the bootstrap attribute of each copied XML at the one in the vendor directory instead: bootstrap="../vendor/typo3/testing-framework/Resources/Core/Build/FunctionalTestsBootstrap.php" from a Build/ beside vendor/.
What a functional test then needs from the installation around it is three more questions: extension-test-extensions, extension-test-site and extension-test-frontend-request.

title: Which Extensions a Functional Test Loads
appliesTo: load an extension in a test
hints: $testExtensionsToLoad takes paths relative to the document root, not to the project root: in a Composer installation with a public/ web directory, "extensions/my_sitepackage" is looked for below public/ and fails with "Test extension path ... not found". Name the extension key or the Composer package name instead — those are resolved against the installed packages, and that is the form a project wants.

Every TYPO3 extension the extension under test requires has to be loaded as well, in $coreExtensionsToLoad or $testExtensionsToLoad. A missing one fails at setup with 'Package "x" depends on package "y" which does not exist' — thrown by the testing framework's own package collection, not by the installation, so it is a test-only failure — and the list to mirror is the extension's own require entries. That makes every requirement a change to every test class: the moment the extension requires one more, each class whose list does not name it fails at setup, including the classes that have nothing to do with what was added.

title: Writing a Site Configuration in a Test
hints: SiteBasedTestTrait is not available. The core's Tests/ directories are export-ignored, so the typo3/cms-core Composer package ships none of them, and the trait every core frontend test builds on cannot be used outside the mono repository. Writing the site configuration in setUp() is what it does anyway.

hints.text: That is one call: $this->get(SiteWriter::class)->write($identifier, $configuration), with the same array the site's config.yaml holds — rootPageId, base, languages, and the sets the site depends on.
That is one call: $this->get(SiteConfiguration::class)->write($identifier, $configuration), with the same array the site's config.yaml holds — rootPageId, base, languages.

hints: That write is not a replace. Where the file already exists it becomes the base, the new array is diffed against it — modified keys applied, keys the array no longer names unset — and the base is read without import processing, so an imports: section is never seen as missing and survives every later write. Which matters here because the test instance is built once per test class and only the database is reset between tests: the configuration one test wrote is what the next one merges into. A class whose tests need different sites writes the whole configuration in setUp(), or removes the file before writing it again.

The file-backed caches live in that instance too — core, typoscript, assets and l10n are file backends, while pages and hash are in the database and do go with the truncation. So a site setting a test changed can still be answered out of the TypoScript the test before it cached, and CacheManager::flushCaches() after writing the configuration is what makes the class deterministic. Both of these fail only in a suite: the test passes when it is run alone with --filter, which is what makes "it works on its own" evidence of nothing.

hints.text: Site settings go into that same array under the settings key, and may be written as flat dotted keys — 'my_ext.products.requestPage' => 4 — as well as as a nested tree, because SiteSettings resolves both and flattens a tree into dotted keys itself. Worth knowing because a set's own settings.yaml uses the nested form, so the flat one looks like it should not work.

setUpFrontendRootPage() and site sets exclude each other. It writes a sys_template row with the clear flag set, and a sys_template that clears resets the AST — dropping the set TypoScript that was included before it. The frontend then answers "No page configured for type=0" and nothing points at the sys_template as the cause. A test whose site takes its TypoScript from a set must not call it, and the settings a plugin needs belong in the pi_flexform of the fixture content element, which is where the site keeps them too.

title: Asserting a Frontend Response in a Test
appliesTo: ID parameter needs to be passed
hints: A frontend response is asserted through $this->executeFrontendSubRequest(new InternalRequest($uri)), which runs the request in the test instance and returns a PSR-7 response. InternalRequest::withQueryParameters() takes scalar values. An Extbase plugin argument is nested two levels deep, so a request that carries one is built with http_build_query() into the URI instead.

A query string built by hand for a cache hash has two more conditions. CacheHashCalculator refuses one that carries relevant parameters without id=<pageId> — 'ID parameter needs to be passed for the cHash calculation!' — and it rawurldecode()s every name and value, which leaves a + as a literal plus where the request the browser sends would have arrived with a space. So encode with PHP_QUERY_RFC3986; otherwise a value containing a space hashes differently than it arrives and the page answers HTTP 404 for something the test never intended to exercise.

title: JavaScript Unit Tests in the Core
hints: The core's JavaScript unit tests live at Build/Sources/TypeScript/<package>/tests/, mirroring the module path below that package, one file per module named with a -test.ts suffix.

Build/web-test-runner.config.mjs makes one group per package under Build/Sources/TypeScript that has a tests/ directory, over tests/**/*.ts. A package without that directory is discovered as nothing, so the first test in one is invisible until the directory exists.

Only backend, core and the rte-ckeditor package carry that directory; form, install, dashboard, filelist and the rest carry none. A suite named for a path in one of those runs over no file, and the first test there creates the group as well as the test. `ls Build/Sources/TypeScript/*/tests` is the check on the branch in hand.

The runner is @web/test-runner, and runTests.sh -s unitJavascript runs it in a container as npm run test inside Build/. That target passes no arguments through, so a targeted or watching run means calling the runner in Build/ directly; npm run watch:test is the same runner with --watch.

The import map in that config points @typo3/core/, @typo3/backend/ and every other package prefix at typo3/sysext/<ext>/Resources/Public/JavaScript/. A test therefore exercises the built output, not the TypeScript source, and a source change is invisible to it until the branch is built.

hints.text: The config serves ~labels/ from a middleware returning { get: key => key }, so a module that reads labels needs no fixture and asserts the key it asked for.

hints: Assertions come from @open-wc/testing, the suite and case functions are mocha's, declared with import type { } from 'mocha'. sinon, axe-core and @web/test-runner-commands are in the same import map.

The modules this layer holds export a class, pure functions, or an object whose methods take their state as arguments, so a test constructs or calls them directly. A collaborator is replaced by stubbing a method on an imported object, as `stub(Icons, 'getIcon')` does. The config loads no module-mocking plugin, so a binding no export reaches cannot be replaced at all.

The older backend modules built on module-level state are the shape it does not hold. EXT:form's form-editor view-model keeps its app and its component references in module-level lets that only `bootstrap()` assigns, and that function runs the whole component setup against the DOM. So no exported function of it can be called on its own, and a missing test on such a module is a cost a review states rather than a change it demands.

This layer sees a module's own state transitions and nothing around them. A defect that only exists inside the real backend — position, stacking, the ancestor chain a component is mounted in — cannot appear in it; browser-tests is the layer that has one.

title: Browser Tests with Playwright
hints: Playwright is where a browser is involved, and the core is the worked example: Build/playwright.config.ts declares the projects and their dependencies, Build/tests/playwright/ holds the suite.

hints.text: Its layout is what transfers: e2e/ for the specs, fixtures/ for the page objects a spec composes itself from, helper/ for the login setup every other project depends on.
Below e2e/ it is one directory per module, and the accessibility scan is a module among them rather than a suite beside them.

Codeception acceptance tests still sit next to it under typo3/sysext/core/Tests/Acceptance/. New specs are written in Playwright; the two suites are not merged, they replace each other module by module.

hints: A backend module renders inside an iframe — id typo3-contentIframe, name list_frame — so every locator in a backend spec goes through page.frameLocator('#typo3-contentIframe'), and one that does not simply matches nothing.

hints.text: A defect that has to be seen rather than asserted — a position, a stacking order, something that only appears while scrolling — is looked at rather than specced first. The core installs the instance the specs run against, publishes it and waits, so the backend can be opened in a browser; typo3_test_run_guide has that suite, what it prints and what the run costs.

hints: browser-test-accessibility is what the same spec can assert, and it is why a site suite must not copy the core's disabled color-contrast rule: contrast is where a theme actually fails and no assertion on the markup sees it. browser-tests-outside-core is the site they run against outside the core, where the specs speak to a real URL and the browsers do not go into the development environment's web container.

A new assertion is evidence once it has been seen to fail: break what it is about, watch it go red, restore, watch it go green. A browser suite needs it more than a unit suite because three shapes pass silently — a locator that matches nothing, a substring the surrounding chrome carries, and an assertion on text the module never emits. project/testing/playwright carries the countermeasure to each.

hints.text: The record list is addressed as /module/content/records, and web_list survives as an identifier alias rather than as a path. A backend spec carried over from an older project therefore names a path that no longer routes there, and what it lands on carries the chrome an assertion on a substring matches. typo3_backend_module_lookup answers what the path is here.

title: Checking Accessibility and Contrast From the Same Spec
hints: Accessibility is checked from the same specs, with @axe-core/playwright: build an AxeBuilder over the page, scan, and assert the violation list is empty. This is the part no PHP test can stand in for, and the one that finds something on the first run.

The core's own scan disables the color-contrast rule, because it scans the backend it also styles. A site suite must not copy that line: contrast is where a theme actually fails. A brand colour that carries a decorative surface fails as text and as a button background, and a disabled control styled with the border grey fails hardest of all — none of which any assertion on the markup can see, because the markup is correct.

The fix for that has a shape: split the palette rather than darken the brand. One custom property for the decorative use, a darker one of the same hue for anything a reader has to read, and the rule that everything textual takes the second — instead of a brand colour bent until it passes everywhere and looks right nowhere.

title: The Site a Project Suite Runs Against
appliesTo: executeFrontendSubRequest is not a browser test
where do the browser tests go
hints: A functional test with executeFrontendSubRequest() runs no JavaScript, applies no stylesheet and speaks no HTTP. It is a rendering test, and calling it a frontend test is how a suite ends up with no browser in it at all. The two are complements: the rendering test asserts what the template produced, the browser test asserts what a reader gets.

Outside the core the layout transfers but the plumbing does not: the specs run against the site as it is served — a real URL, the development environment's own — rather than against a per-test-class instance, and the browsers belong on the host or in an image of their own. Installing them into the web container of a development environment is the step to skip.

The suite is a project of its own in playwright.config.ts, with the login setup declared as a dependency so the authenticated state is written once and reused. Give the site's page types one spec each — that is the list that finds a page layout nobody rendered since the template changed.

Where that configuration and those specs live in a project is the repository's question rather than the extension's — the specs need a running site, so they belong to what is deployed. The project repository layout hint has it. In a repository that is only the extension there is no such split, and the suite belongs to the package like everything else there.

title: Setting Up PHPStan for an Extension
hints: The configuration belongs to the package, in Build/phpstan/ beside the phpunit configurations the test setup already put there. typo3/testing-framework is the setup worth reading: it is a TYPO3 package with no core mono repository around it, which is the situation an extension is in. Its paths are the package's own Classes and Tests directories, and it includes the phpstan-phpunit extension so test code is understood as tests rather than as ordinary classes.

Set tmpDir to a path inside the repository. PHPStan otherwise writes its result cache to /tmp/phpstan, every checkout on the machine shares that one directory, and the cache stores absolute paths — so a checkout that has been deleted since fails the analysis of every other one, with an internal error naming a path the caller has never seen. The core and typo3/testing-framework both set it, and both explain it in the same words: a local cache dir instead of /tmp. CI is the exception the core makes in a second configuration file that overrides it back to /tmp, because that container is discarded after the run and caching it buys nothing.

TYPO3 defines constants at runtime that the analysis never gets to see, so they are declared in a file named under bootstrapFiles — LF and CR, and ORIGINAL_ROOT where the test setup uses it. Without it every use of them is reported as an undefined constant, which is a wall of findings about code that is correct.

ext_emconf.php is excluded rather than fixed. It assigns into $_EXTKEY, which the file including it sets, so the analysis reports the variable as undefined; typo3/testing-framework excludes the ext_emconf.php of its fixture extensions for exactly that reason.

A baseline is what makes the first run usable. Generating one records every finding that is already there into phpstan-baseline.neon, which the configuration includes first, so the run reports what a change added rather than what the package accumulated before anyone looked. It is a work list, not a suppression: an entry that disappears is removed from the file by regenerating it.

The core and typo3/testing-framework both analyse at level 5. Levels are cumulative, so raising one on a package that has never been analysed produces the whole difference at once — which is what the baseline is for.

title: Satisfying PHPStan in a Core Patch
hints: Where a signature is wider than what the code actually has, the core narrows with a `/** @var Type $variable */` line directly above the assignment, not with a cast and not with an `instanceof` check. `CacheManager::getCache()` is declared to return `FrontendInterface`, so handing its result to a parameter typed `PhpFrontend` is an `argument.type` finding; `TYPO3\CMS\Core\TypoScript\TypoScriptStringFactory` and `TYPO3\CMS\Core\Core\Bootstrap` narrow it that way in production code and `RedirectServiceTest` does the same in a functional test. The inline `@var` is written throughout `Classes/` and `Tests/` while `assert($value instanceof …)` is written nowhere, so it is the codebase's idiom rather than the habit of those files.

An `instanceof` check belongs where the value arrives from outside and the code cannot know which it is: `ContainerBuilder::createDependencyInjectionContainer()` takes a `FrontendInterface` parameter and throws where it is not a `PhpFrontend`. Where the call itself decides what comes back, the same check guards a case that cannot happen.

A `@var` narrows within the declared type and may not contradict it — `PHPDoc tag @var with type X is not subtype of native type Y` is `varTag.nativeType`. The analysis runs at level 5 with `treatPhpDocTypesAsCertain: false`, so the annotation is taken for the argument check without a later condition on the same value being reported as always true.

A service taken from the container is typed already: `bnf/phpstan-psr-container` reads a `ContainerInterface::get()` call by the class name handed in, and a functional test case is itself a `ContainerInterface`, so `$this->get(CacheManager::class)` is a `CacheManager`. A cache taken by a string identifier is typed by nothing, which is why the container call in front of `getCache('typoscript')` needs no annotation and the assignment behind it does.

`instanceof` against a variable already typed `X|null` is rejected by the core's own `UnneededInstanceOfRule` with `Unneeded instanceof on X|null. Use a null check instead.`, under the identifier `instanceof.unneededNotNullSubstitute`. What it asks for is `!== null`.

hints.text: `unserialize()` is called with its `$options` argument and `allowed_classes` set to `false` or to a list of class names. `UnserializeRule` rejects the call that omits the argument, the one passing `true`, a `max_depth` that is not an integer, and any other key; its identifiers all begin `unserialize.`.

A named argument in a method or static call is rejected by `NamedArgumentUsageRule` under `custom.namedArguments`, and the message names every optional parameter the call skipped. `TYPO3\CMS\Core\Tests`, `TYPO3\CMS\Extbase\Tests` and `TYPO3\CMS\Frontend\Tests` are exempt, and a constructor call is neither a method nor a static call, so `new Foo(bar: 1)` passes anywhere.
`#[WithoutErrorHandler]` is forbidden on a class and on a method by `ForbidAttributeRule`, under `attribute.forbidden.classScope` and `attributes.forbidden.methodScope`.

hints: Only `typo3/sysext/` is analysed, from `Build/phpstan/phpstan.neon`, so no finding comes out of `Build/` or the repository root. Three things inside it are excluded and stay excluded: the install tool's ExtensionScanner matcher fixtures, every `ext_emconf.php`, and the Extbase reflection fixture whose syntax is broken on purpose.

The configuration includes `phpstan-baseline.neon` before everything else, so a finding recorded there is one that already existed. Whether a file carries an entry is read from the `path:` keys, which are written relative to `Build/phpstan/` as `../../typo3/sysext/…`; finding none is the ordinary answer and means the run reported the patch's own finding rather than an inherited one.

hints.text: The core's own `AGENTS.md` forbids silencing a new static-analysis finding in `Build/phpstan/phpstan-baseline.neon`, because the baseline is meant to shrink, and allows regenerating it with `-s phpstanGenerateBaseline` only after a PHPStan update.

title: Setting Up the Coding Standards Fixer for an Extension
hints: The rule set is typo3/coding-standards, required as a development dependency, and it is a php-cs-fixer configuration rather than a checker of its own — installing it pulls friendsofphp/php-cs-fixer in with it. The package is still below its first major release, so a caret constraint covers one minor and no more: the next release is an edit to composer.json rather than a composer update. Which release resolves is decided by the PHP floor the extension still supports, because the package raises its own php requirement release by release and an extension whose declared range still reaches an older PHP resolves to an older one. Read that off composer show typo3/coding-standards rather than copying a constraint out of another project.

composer exec typo3-coding-standards setup writes the boilerplate, and the package ships that binary and the shorter t3-cs for the same console. The type argument is optional and detected from composer.json: a type of typo3-cms-extension or a non-empty extra.typo3/cms.extension-key makes it extension, anything else project. --rule-set defaults to both sets, so a bare setup writes .editorconfig and .php-cs-fixer.dist.php at once, and passing it once selects one. --target-dir puts them somewhere other than the Composer root. A file that is already there is refused with a message and a non-zero exit rather than overwritten, which --force is for, and a legacy .php_cs or .php-cs-fixer.php is renamed to the dist name instead of being left beside it.

The two templates differ in one line: the extension one is CsFixerConfig::create() with $config->getFinder()->in(__DIR__), the whole package directory, while the project one scans __DIR__ . '/src'. PhpCsFixer\Finder already restricts that scan to *.php, excludes vendor and ignores dot files and VCS directories; CsFixerConfig::create() adds .build, typo3temp and var to the excludes and config/system/settings.php to notPath. An exclude entry is a directory name matched at any depth and case-sensitively, so Classes/var/ is out while Vendor/ is in.

What ->in(__DIR__) still reaches is a build directory or document root that is neither hidden nor one of the excluded names: build/ or public/ is scanned, the installer's own index.php among it, and naming the first-party paths explicitly is the answer there. The configuration file is a dot file, so the fixer never formats its own configuration.

Checking and fixing are one command with one option and two exit codes. php-cs-fixer fix rewrites and exits 0 whether it changed anything or not, so it can never be the check; php-cs-fixer fix --dry-run --diff writes nothing and exits 8 where a file would change, 0 where none would. Declare the two as separate commands, because a CI step calling the fixing one is green on a tree it has just rewritten.

.editorconfig is a copy rather than a dependency. Updating the package brings new fixer rules in immediately while that file stays whatever was copied, and typo3-coding-standards update is what rewrites it — overwriting local edits without asking, so it is run against a committed tree. The shipped file indents with four spaces by default, two for YAML, TypoScript, XLF and TypeScript, and a tab for JSON and .htaccess, so a check introduced over an existing tree finds the XLF and JSON files first. Nothing in the package checks it: editorconfig-checker is a separate tool.
extension-static-analysis is the other half of this layer: where the analyser's configuration belongs, the constants it never sees, its result cache and its baseline.

title: Unit Tests, Test Doubles and Data Providers in PHPUnit
hints: A unit test exercises one small part and nothing outside the process it runs in. It starts no database, no container and no subprocess, makes no HTTP request, and writes into no directory the repository keeps. That is what makes a red test mean the code changed rather than the machine did: the same suite has to answer the same on a laptop with nothing installed. Where a class reaches outside, the way past is a seam in that class — a collaborator it takes rather than creates — and where there is no seam, making one is part of the work rather than a reason to write a test that starts the real thing. TYPO3 splits this by base class: TYPO3\TestingFramework\Core\Unit\UnitTestCase for the isolated ones, TYPO3\TestingFramework\Core\Functional\FunctionalTestCase for what genuinely needs a database and an installation.

Arranging the real thing where the test can find it is still a dependency on the machine. Writing an executable into a temporary directory and putting that directory on the PATH looks like a mock and is not one: it depends on the directory being writable, on chmod, and on a /tmp nobody mounted noexec, and the code under test still forks a shell. The same applies to writing fixture files into the package's own directories and deleting them afterwards — a run that dies in between leaves them behind, in the directories the next run reads. UnitTestCase::$testFilesToDelete exists for files a test cannot avoid writing, and the better answer is usually not to write them.

Stub when the double only has to answer, mock when the call itself is what you are asserting. self::createStub(SomeInterface::class) returns a double with no expectations; self::createMock(SomeInterface::class) adds expects($this->once())->method('x')->with(...), which fails the test when the call does not happen or happens with other arguments. The distinction is worth keeping: a stub carrying expectations turns an unrelated refactoring into a failing test about a call nobody was asserting. The core's own unit tests reach for the stub markedly more often than for the mock, which is the ratio to expect when most doubles are there to answer rather than to be checked.

The verbs on a configured method are willReturn(), willReturnMap() for a table of arguments to results, willReturnCallback() where the answer depends on what was passed, willReturnOnConsecutiveCalls() where one method is called several times in a known order, willReturnSelf() for fluent interfaces and willThrowException(). self::createConfiguredStub($class, ['method' => $value]) is the short form for a double answering a few methods with fixed values. withConsecutive() is gone from current PHPUnit and has no replacement of the same shape: express it with willReturnCallback() recording what it was handed, and assert on the record afterwards.

Several inputs to one behaviour belong in a data provider rather than in a foreach inside the test. A failure then names the case instead of a position in a loop, and the run reports how many of them there are. The provider is a public static method returning an array keyed by a sentence describing the case, and it is bound with the #[PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider('providerName')] attribute — the core uses the attribute throughout its unit tests and the older @dataProvider annotation nowhere, so the attribute is what a patch is written against. A loop is still right where the cases are not inputs but a corpus the test walks: every registered icon, every file in a directory, every entry of a configuration. There the assertion message carries the offending name and one failure is the whole answer.

Which PHPUnit is available is not a free choice in an extension. It is decided by the oldest typo3/testing-framework the extension still supports, so the constraint to read before reaching for a newer API is that package's requirement rather than what the core happens to be on.
